hints: Work backwards from the products $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, both contain a straight chain of three carbons, so think about which $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}$ isomer can be oxidised to both.
walkthrough:
Use the oxidation products to find the alcohol**
Look at what you are given. Both products have three carbons in a straight line: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Only a primary alcohol with the OH on the end carbon can be oxidised first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid with the same carbon skeleton. That must be $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, propan-1-ol.

Draw it as a skeletal formula**
In skeletal formulae carbon atoms are the corners and ends of lines, and hydrogens on carbon are hidden. For propan-1-ol draw a zig-zag of two lines (three carbons) and put an OH group on the end carbon. So it looks like a bent two-line chain ending in OH.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, propan-1-ol, drawn as skeletal: three-carbon zig-zag with OH on the end carbon.

hints: Reaction 1 converts propan-1-ol all the way to propanoic acid, so identify the strong oxidising agent used for full oxidation of primary alcohols.
Think about the apparatus needed to keep the intermediate aldehyde in the reaction mixture so it can be oxidised further, rather than letting it escape.
walkthrough:
Recognise full oxidation**
You are starting from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and finishing at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. That is oxidation in two stages, alcohol to aldehyde to acid. The standard AS oxidant for this is acidified dichromate, written as $\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ or acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$.

Choose reflux to keep everything in**
If you heat in an open vessel the aldehyde intermediate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, would boil off before it can react further. Heating under reflux condenses any vapour and returns it to the flask, so the aldehyde stays in contact with the oxidant and is oxidised on to the carboxylic acid.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate, $\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$; heat under reflux.

hints: Reaction 2 stops at the aldehyde $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, so the oxidising agent is the same as for full oxidation, think about which reagent that is.
Think about how to remove the aldehyde from the oxidising mixture as soon as it forms, using its lower boiling point, so it cannot be oxidised further.
walkthrough:
Recognise partial oxidation**
Here you want to stop at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. You still need a strong oxidant to convert the primary alcohol to the aldehyde, so use the same reagent: acidified dichromate, $\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$.

Distil the aldehyde away**
The trick is in the condition. The aldehyde has a lower boiling point than the alcohol and acid because it has no hydrogen bonding between its own molecules. If you gently heat and distil, the aldehyde vapour is collected and condensed into a separate receiver as soon as it forms. Removed from the oxidant, it cannot be oxidised further to the acid.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate, $\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$; heat and distil (immediate distillation).

hints: Reaction 3 joins $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ with loss of water, recall the family of product formed from an acid plus an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Spot esterification and name the ester**
A carboxylic acid plus an alcohol gives an ester plus water: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. To name it, take the acid part first as propanoate (from propanoic acid) and the alcohol part as propyl (from propanol). Together this gives propyl propanoate.
